title: 100% Tariff Threat Sharpens India's Push for Trade Deals Beyond the U.S.
excerpt: With Washington poised to authorize tariffs of up to 100% on Russian oil buyers, India is racing to diversify through new trade pacts with the UK and EU — but economists doubt they can quickly replace the American market.
body:
• The U.S. Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by 86-11, and the House is moving toward final passage — the bill would let Washington impose tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, a group that includes India.
  • India already faces a combined 50% U.S. tariff: a 25% baseline plus an additional 25% penalty tied to its Russian oil purchases, in place since August 2025.
  • New Delhi's hedge is a burst of trade diplomacy — the India-UK pact took effect July 15, 2026 with duty-free access for 99% of Indian exports, and an India-EU free trade agreement is in its final stretch with a signing expected before year-end.
  • Analysts caution the deals are no quick substitute: the U.S. remains India's largest export market, and India imports over 88% of its crude, having saved an estimated $12.6 billion on discounted Russian oil since 2022.

A new front in the tariff war

India's trade relationship with the United States is facing its gravest threat yet. A bipartisan Russia sanctions bill that cleared the U.S. Senate 86-11 and has advanced in the House would give the Trump administration authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the largest importers of Russian oil and gas — a list that includes India, the largest single importer of Russian seaborne crude.

The bill does not impose the rate automatically. The U.S. Trade Representative would set the actual tariff country by country, and the president could waive the measures by certifying the decision to Congress, subject to review every 180 days. For Indian exporters already paying a combined 50% U.S. duty, the legislation opens the door to a rate that would shut them out of the American market.

Eighteen months of escalation

The confrontation has been building since February 2025, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Washington visit launched formal talks on an India-U.S. bilateral trade agreement. What followed reads like a tariff rollercoaster: a 26% U.S. duty announced on Indian imports in April 2025, a 25% rate in July, and the additional 25% penalty in August 2025 tied to India's Russian oil purchases — bringing the combined tariff to 50%.

New Delhi calls the oil-linked penalty unfair, arguing its purchases are driven by energy security. India imports over 88% of its crude, with most of it coming from just six countries, and its strategic reserves cover only 9 to 10 days of net imports — against roughly 200 days in Japan. The Council on Energy, Environment and Water estimates India has saved about $12.6 billion from its post-2022 shift to discounted Russian crude.

Can new deals offset the U.S. market?

Against this backdrop, India's newly concluded trade agreements look like a deliberate diversification strategy. The India-UK trade pact took effect on July 15, 2026, giving Indian exporters duty-free access to about 99% of British tariff lines — zeroing duties of up to 70% on processed foods, 21.5% on marine products, 18% on engineering goods, and 12% on textiles, according to Reuters.

The larger prize is the European Union. India and the EU concluded FTA negotiations on January 27, 2026, and on September 11 the European Commission moved to seek approval to sign and conclude the pact, targeting signature before the end of 2026 and implementation early in 2027. The Commission estimates the deal would eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96% of EU goods exports to India, while Indian exporters in textiles, engineering, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and processed food gain improved access to the 27-nation bloc.

"China has massive leverage over the global economy, particularly through its dominance of critical supply chains. India, despite being one of the world's biggest economies, does not have the same leverage."

— Michael Kugelman, South Asia analyst

Diaspora angle

For Indian-American investors and businesses, the stakes are direct: India-focused equity funds have shown sensitivity to each twist in the tariff saga, and small U.S. businesses that source textiles, jewellery or seafood from India face rising input costs if duties climb again.

"India should not allow US tariff threats to determine its energy policy. It should continue buying Russian oil as long as it remains commercially competitive."

— Ajay Srivastava, founder, Global Trade Research Initiative

What's next

The immediate question is the House vote. If the bill reaches President Donald Trump, the U.S. Trade Representative would determine actual tariff rates — a process that could turn the 100% figure into a negotiating lever against Delhi. Parallel to that, the India-EU signing is targeted for December, with implementation as early as February or March 2027. Whether that expanding web of deals can genuinely reduce India's dependence on the American market will be the defining trade question of 2027.
image_caption: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal gestures while speaking at an industry event in New Delhi. Goyal is steering India's push for new trade deals as the US threatens tariffs of up to 100% on top buyers of Russian energy.
nri_angle: Indian-American investors and small businesses sourcing from India face rising costs and portfolio exposure as tariffs climb, while the UK and EU pacts may redirect where Indian exporters sell.
author: Diaspora Desk
